lessons.title: You ask. AI answers.
lessons.subtitle: Start with the AI tools you already know.
lessons.objective: Recognize a prompt and an output, then see how AI, ML, and deep learning fit together.

steps.title: Prompt and output
paragraphs: You already use ChatGPT, Claude Code, and Codex. We can begin with something you do every day: sending a message and receiving a reply.
A prompt is the message you give an AI. The output is what it gives back. An output can be a picture, a written reply, or code.
example: Make a picture of a red car.
steps.takeaway: Prompt = what you send. Output = what comes back.

steps.title: What does AI mean?
paragraphs: AI stands for artificial intelligence. It is a broad field of making computers do tasks such as recognizing pictures or understanding language.
A computer does not need human feelings or understanding to produce a useful answer. Its answer can still be wrong, so we check the result.
example: You ask for a red car.
steps.takeaway: A confident answer still needs checking.

steps.title: The AI family
paragraphs: Machine learning, or ML, is one way of building AI. We use examples to adjust a model. A model is a mathematical system that turns an input into an output.
Deep learning is a kind of machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers. A neural network is a set of connected calculations.
Think of boxes inside boxes. Deep learning fits inside ML, and ML fits inside AI. Some AI methods do not use ML.
steps.takeaway: Deep learning is part of ML. ML is part of AI.

practice.title: Write your own image request
practice.instruction: Write one short prompt for an image you would like. On the next line, describe what you would check in the finished image.

quiz.text: You type “Make a picture of a red car.” What is that message?
quiz.explanation: The message you give the AI is the prompt.

quiz.text: The AI gives you a picture. What is the picture?
quiz.explanation: The picture is the result the AI produced: its output.

quiz.text: Which is the broadest field?
quiz.explanation: AI is the broad field. ML and deep learning sit inside it.

quiz.text: A reply sounds confident. What should you do?
quiz.explanation: Confidence does not prove correctness. Check the result.

lessons.title: Give your work a home.
lessons.subtitle: Understand files, folders, and saving.
lessons.objective: Explain the difference between a file and a folder, and describe where your practice belongs.

steps.title: Files and folders
paragraphs: A file is one saved item, such as a photo, a lesson, or a program. A folder is a container that holds files and other folders.
Think of a file as one page and a folder as the binder that holds the pages.
steps.takeaway: A file holds content. A folder keeps items together.

steps.title: What is a path?
paragraphs: A path tells the computer where an item is. It is like an address for a file.
Your course lives in D:\AI Engineering Academy. Your small coding attempts belong in 02_Practice. The name at the end of a path identifies the file.
steps.takeaway: Read a path from the larger location toward the file.

steps.title: Save before you run
paragraphs: Editing changes what you see in the editor. Saving writes that change to the file. In VS Code, Ctrl+S saves the open file.
If you change a sentence but run an older saved version, the computer may still show the old sentence. Check the file name and save again.
steps.takeaway: Edit, save, then run.

practice.title: Find your practice folder
practice.instruction: Open your academy folder in File Explorer. Find 02_Practice. In your own words, write what belongs in this folder and how a file differs from a folder.
practice.placeholder:
A file is ...
A folder is ...
02_Practice is for ...

quiz.text: Which item is a file?
quiz.explanation: chair.png is one saved item: a file.

quiz.text: What does a folder do?
quiz.explanation: Folders organize files and other folders.

quiz.text: What does a path describe?
quiz.explanation: A path gives the location of an item.

quiz.text: You changed code in VS Code. What should you do before running it?
quiz.explanation: Save so the computer runs the changed file.

lessons.title: Run your first Python.
lessons.subtitle: Tell the computer to show a sentence.
lessons.objective: Predict and run a print instruction, then change it yourself.

steps.title: A program is instructions
paragraphs: A program is a set of instructions a computer can run. Python is the programming language we will start with.
Code does not need AI to be useful. A program can simply follow the instructions you write.
steps.takeaway: Code tells the computer what to do.

steps.title: Meet print
paragraphs: print asks Python to show something. The quotation marks tell Python where your text begins and ends.
The parentheses hold what you give to print. Before running this line, predict what you will see.
example: The quotation marks do not appear in the output.
steps.takeaway: print shows text or a value.

steps.title: Change one thing
paragraphs: Run the example in the practice pad. Then change the sentence to something you want to say and run it again.
A mistake is useful information. If you see an error, read it and check the quotes and parentheses. You can ask the tutor for one hint.
steps.takeaway: Predict, run, compare, then change.

practice.title: Make Python say something you choose
practice.instruction: First run this demonstration. Then change the text to your own sentence and run it again. The pad supports print, variables, and simple arithmetic.

quiz.text: What does print do?
quiz.explanation: print displays text or values.

quiz.text: What appears after print("Hello")?
quiz.explanation: The quotes mark the text in code; they are not printed.

quiz.text: What is Python?
quiz.explanation: Python is a language for writing programs.

quiz.text: You see an error. What is a useful next step?
options: Read the message and check the relevant line
quiz.explanation: Error messages give clues. Start with the line they point to.

lessons.title: Predict before you run.
lessons.subtitle: Follow a program one line at a time.
lessons.objective: Predict printed text and simple arithmetic results.

steps.title: Order matters
paragraphs: For these simple programs, Python follows each line from top to bottom. The first print appears before the second.
Tracing means following the instructions in your head. Predicting first helps you notice when your understanding differs from the result.
steps.takeaway: Follow one line, then the next.

steps.title: Text or a calculation?
paragraphs: Text inside quotes is called a string. Python prints it as text. A calculation without quotes can produce a number.
Compare the two lines. One shows the symbols 2 + 3. The other calculates their total.
steps.takeaway: Quotes make text. Without quotes, 2 + 3 is a calculation.

steps.title: Your prediction is evidence
paragraphs: A surprising result does not mean you are bad at coding. It shows exactly which idea to investigate.
Write your prediction, run the code, and compare. Change one small part to test what you think it does.
steps.takeaway: A prediction makes a useful experiment.

practice.title: Try text and numbers
practice.instruction: Predict both lines before running. Then choose different numbers and compare text with a calculation.

quiz.text: What does print(2 + 3) show?
quiz.explanation: Without quotes, Python adds the numbers.

quiz.text: What does print("2 + 3") show?
quiz.explanation: The quoted characters are printed as text.

quiz.text: Which line runs first in our simple examples?
quiz.explanation: These instructions run from top to bottom.

quiz.text: Why predict before running?
options: To compare your understanding with the result
quiz.explanation: Comparing a prediction with the result helps you learn.

lessons.title: Rules and learned patterns.
lessons.subtitle: See two ways a computer can make a decision.
lessons.objective: Distinguish a written rule from learning from examples.

steps.title: A rule you write
paragraphs: Imagine sorting images by file name. You write a rule: if a name contains chair, put it in the chair group.
The computer follows that exact rule. It does not discover a visual pattern from training photos.
example: A table photo named chair.png goes in the chair group.
steps.takeaway: A written rule follows the condition you specify.

steps.title: Learning from examples
paragraphs: Instead, you could show a model many photos labeled chair or table. Training adjusts its settings using those examples.
Then you test it on different photos. This is important: remembering training examples does not prove it will work on new ones.
steps.takeaway: Training uses examples. Testing checks different examples.

steps.title: Both approaches have limits
paragraphs: A simple written rule can be a good choice for a clear task. Machine learning can help when patterns are harder to describe by hand.
Both can fail. An engineer checks the result and chooses an approach that fits the task. More complicated is not automatically better.
steps.takeaway: Pick a suitable approach, then test it.

practice.title: Spot a weakness in a rule
practice.instruction: A program puts every file whose name contains cat into a cat-photo group. Describe one case where this rule could give a wrong result.
practice.placeholder: The rule could be wrong when ...

quiz.text: A developer writes every sorting condition. What is the program using?
quiz.explanation: The developer supplied the conditions explicitly.

quiz.text: What does training use to adjust a model?
quiz.explanation: Training adjusts a model using data or examples.

quiz.text: Why test on different photos?
options: To make the app look nicer
To see how it handles new examples
quiz.explanation: Unseen examples help check generalization.

quiz.text: Which approach can make mistakes?
quiz.explanation: Both rules and learned models can fail.

lessons.title: Find your first bug.
lessons.subtitle: Use an error as a clue.
lessons.objective: Find a missing quote and explain why the change fixes it.

steps.title: What is a bug?
paragraphs: A bug is a problem in a program. Debugging means finding the cause and fixing it.
An error message gives you a clue. Start with the line it mentions and compare it with a working example.
steps.takeaway: Find the cause before changing lots of things.

steps.title: Look for pairs
paragraphs: Our print instructions need paired quotation marks and parentheses. If a quote is missing, Python cannot tell where the text ends.
Look carefully at this broken line. Do not change the words yet. Find what is missing.
steps.takeaway: A missing character can change how code is read.

steps.title: Change, run, explain
paragraphs: Make one small change, run the code again, and compare the result with what you wanted.
Explain why the change worked. That explanation is more useful than copying a corrected line without understanding it.
steps.takeaway: A fix is stronger when you can explain it.

practice.title: Repair this line
practice.instruction: Run the broken code once to read the error. Then fix the missing character and run it again. Tell the tutor what you changed and why.

quiz.text: What does debugging mean?
quiz.explanation: Debugging is investigating the cause and fixing it.

quiz.text: What should you read when code fails?
quiz.explanation: The error message often points toward the problem.

quiz.text: Why change one small thing first?
options: It helps identify what affected the result
quiz.explanation: Small changes make causes easier to track.

quiz.text: After a fix, what should you do?
options: Run it and check the result
quiz.explanation: Run the corrected code to verify the behavior.

lessons.title: Your first checkpoint.
lessons.subtitle: Bring your first week together.
lessons.objective: Explain an AI interaction, run a small program, and identify what still needs practice.

steps.title: What you can explain
paragraphs: A prompt goes to an AI; an output comes back. AI is the broad field, ML learns patterns from examples, and deep learning is a kind of ML.
A file is one saved item. A folder holds items. Python runs instructions, and print can show text.
steps.takeaway: Use your own words. You do not need a memorized definition.

steps.title: A tiny demonstration
paragraphs: Build a small welcome program in the practice pad. It should print a greeting and one thing you want to learn.
Choose your own sentences. Before running, predict both lines. After running, explain what print does.
steps.takeaway: Your own attempt is the evidence.

steps.title: Be honest about readiness
paragraphs: A quiz score is useful, but it does not prove you can build independently. Ask the tutor to check your explanation and your code.
If something is unclear, practice it again. Completing this page records a classroom activity; it does not automatically award professional skills or a level badge.
steps.takeaway: Move forward when the foundations make sense.

practice.title: Build your welcome program
practice.instruction: Write your own two print instructions: a greeting and something you want to learn. The pad is blank so you can make your own attempt.

quiz.text: An AI writes a reply. What is the reply called?
quiz.explanation: The reply is the result produced by the AI.

quiz.text: Which statement describes the groups correctly?
options: Deep learning is part of ML, which is part of AI
quiz.explanation: The groups fit inside one another.

quiz.text: What should you do before running an edited file?
quiz.explanation: Saving writes the edited version to disk.

quiz.text: What is useful evidence of understanding?
options: Explaining and checking your own work
quiz.explanation: Your explanation and tested attempt show understanding.
